1	# The report and the record
2	
3	## What every report holds
4	
5	Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.
6	
7	A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.
8	
9	A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.
10	
11	A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.
12	
13	Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:
14	
15	- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
16	- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
17	- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
18	- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
19	- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
20	- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
21	- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.
22	
23	## At a point to report
24	
25	- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
26	- Then finish the work.
27	- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.
28	
29	## Timings and citations
30	
31	- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
32	- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
33	- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
34	- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.
35	
36	## POSITIONS and FACTS
37	
38	POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.
39	
40	Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".
41	
42	## The gap ledger
43	
44	The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).
45	
46	A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.
47	
48	- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
49	- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
50	- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.
51	
52	Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.
53	
54	A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.
55	
56	The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.
57	
58	## Reading the record
59	
60	Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:
61	
62	    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh
63	
64	- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
65	- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
66	- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
67	- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
68	- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
69	- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
70	- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
71	- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.
72	
73	A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.
74	
75	Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:
76	
77	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE
78	
79	## Writing to the record
80	
81	- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
82	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
83	- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
84	  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
85	  - what it means for the work;
86	  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
87	  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
88	  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
89	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
90	- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
91	- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.
92	
93	Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.
94	
95	    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"
96	
97	To add a row:
98	
99	1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
100	2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
101	3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.
102	
103	To change a row:
104	
105	- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters. `$L note N TEXT --check` writes nothing. It says whether TEXT fits, and how many characters the notes and the row have left now and would have left with TEXT. These counts include the separator that the tool adds. It exits 0 if TEXT fits, and 1 if not. Run it before a long note, or before a note on a row near its limits. If TEXT does not fit, shorten it, or cut the notes with `rewrite` (below).
106	- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
107	- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
108	- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
109	- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.
110	
111	## The repository's history
112	
113	- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
114	- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
115	- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
116	- If the commands above fail, run `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository`. It prints `true` in a shallow clone, where these commits do not resolve. There, a copyright header of Sun Microsystems or Oracle, as in `Library/Format.fss`, marks a file that the team made, but not which of its lines the port or the revival changed. If your task needs those lines, say in your report that the clone is shallow.
117	- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
118	- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
119	- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.

1	# Keeping the record
2	
3	How workers read the record, and edit it when a brief asks, is `fortress-repo`'s records part.
4	
5	**history**
6	: `FACTS-history.md` or `POSITIONS-history.md`. Under each number, one block per change: a provenance line (the time, the kind of change, the report section, the commit, who, why) and the line as it stood before.
7	
8	**pointer**
9	: Another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, with a few words on its subject: "It builds P-48, on a type parameter that a call does not fix."
10	
11	**pass**
12	: Your rewrite of what a worker wrote into entries of the form below.
13	
14	## What an entry is
15	
16	An entry reads on its own. A reader who knows the language, or can look it up in the `fortress-repo` skill, can tell what it says without the conversation or the batch behind it. The entry lets a worker or you act right without opening the report, and says when the report is needed. Its number is permanent and never reused. Its title and text are rewritten freely, since the number is the key.
17	
18	- A FACTS entry holds, after its number and a bold title that states the fact: what is established now, and under which conditions; what it means for the work, such as what it blocks or which row or decision it bears on; its evidence: the test that gates it, or its source, and whether it was observed, read in the code or inferred; the decision it builds, by number and subject; and the report section that holds the detail.
19	- A POSITIONS entry holds, after its number and a bold title: what the curator decided about the project, and why, in one or two sentences; where it applies; and what it requires of the work. It may point to a fact that it rests on, in the sentence that needs it. `P-48+` finds every fact that points to it.
20	- A POSITIONS entry states the curator's meaning in the record's register, and every fact in it is correct. It is the smallest text from which a fresh worker or coordinator, with the skills loaded, decides right. Workers and you decide by it where the curator is not asked, so a wrong premise in it spreads to each of those decisions.
21	- Give as an entry's reason the ground of its own case, such as the specification's text, the library's code or a measurement. Never give a rule that holds for every decision, such as the team's later word (P-26).
22	- POSITIONS holds only the curator's decisions. A choice that a worker made and landed without the curator's word is a fact about the tree. Its FACTS entry says that a worker chose it. If the choice is consequential, its review-queue item names that entry.
23	- An entry states the present, or what holds for all time. It holds no plan and no status: no state words such as "Built." or "Still to build:", no PLAN phase or item, no review-queue item, and no words that it waits for the curator's review. PLAN and the review queue name the entries that their items concern.
24	- If the tree does not yet do what a decision or the team's design asks, the missing part is a row of the gap ledger. The entry may name it as "row N", with a few words on what the row holds. In an entry, "row N" always names a row of the gap ledger.
25	- A pointer that stays in an entry carries a few words on what it holds, such as a ledger row's subject. A bare list of numbers goes to the history.
26	- A handle that only made sense in a past conversation, such as "answer 9", goes to the history.
27	- Quote the curator only where the exact words are the decision. Otherwise condense the words into the position, keeping the part of the rule that cuts. Check the condensed text against the words before you write it. The dictated words go to the history, with their time.
28	- A count that each landing changes has one entry with its current value, what it counts, the kinds with the largest share, and how to read a move. Other entries give its number. A count from one measurement says so.
29	- An entry holds one claim that can be kept up to date on its own, with its conditions, exceptions and evidence. Split an entry when its claims answer different questions and change apart. Before you split, look for an entry that already holds the claim, and move the text there. After a split, grep the record for the old number, and repoint each pointer that meant the claim that moved.
30	- If several entries together establish a conclusion that workers keep working out again, make it a sentence of the entry that owns its subject, with pointers to the entries it rests on. The pass updates it when one of them changes. Add a new entry only if no entry owns it. Leave a conclusion nobody has checked in its report, out of the entries.
31	- Keep an entry near 600 characters. This is a check, not a cap, and no reason to split: an entry may pass it if a question below keeps a sentence.
32	- Write halfway to ASD-STE100.
33	
34	Ask of each sentence, and act on the answer:
35	
36	1. Would the reader do otherwise without it? Keep it.
37	2. Would the reader misread another sentence without it? Keep it.
38	3. Does it tell how the fact came about: a date, a batch, a correction? Move it to the history.
39	4. Is it detail needed only while doing the work: a line number, a list of sites, a timing? Leave it in the report, and name the section.
40	5. Does another entry or a skill say it? Give that entry's number, or the skill's part.
41	6. Can a reader new to the project follow every word? Name the kind of each count.
42	
43	In a consolidation of FACTS, judge each entry by six checks. Mark each one pass, fail, or unresolved where evidence is still needed, and quote the passage that fails:
44	
45	- Scope: the title and the text agree on the path, the conditions and the limits, and claim no more than the evidence shows.
46	- Present meaning: a reader can tell the current property, or a measurement bounded to its day, without rebuilding a batch's work.
47	- Evidence: the cited support exists and holds the claim, and the entry states the kind of its evidence and its uncertainty.
48	- Comprehension: a reader can restate the fact and what it means. Subjects, referents and terms are plain.
49	- Ownership: the entry has one subject. No repair history or copied count hides it.
50	- Consistency: entries on the same subject agree, or state their different scopes or their conflict.
51	
52	An entry that fails scope, evidence or consistency is not kept as it stands: reword it to what its support holds, or investigate where the support is unresolved. A fail of comprehension or ownership asks for a rewrite. Give no score: good prose does not make up for an unsupported claim. Then give the entry one disposition:
53	
54	- keep: every check passes;
55	- reword: the meaning holds, but the wording or the stated scope fails;
56	- reorganize: move detail out, merge the entry into its owner, or split it;
57	- investigate: the support or the consistency is unresolved. Settle that narrow question before any new wording, and do not delete the fact meanwhile.
58	
59	Before you write or check the first entries of a consolidation, read the five worked examples: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-rule-draft.md#Worked examples'`, a large read.
60	
61	## Reading and writing
62	
63	- `git log -S'F-87' --oneline -- explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md` lists the commits that touched an entry.
64	- To read a history in depth, or a report's passage, send a Sonnet scout. The provenance lines tell it where to dig.
65	- `record.py`'s header gives its usage. `add`, `set`, `merge`, `remove` and `apply` write; each needs `--from PATH#HEADING` or `--note WHY`. The tool stamps the time and copies the earlier line to the history.
66	- Before every commit, run `record.py check --base <the commit before your edits>`. It shows that nothing was lost, and reports each entry over 600 characters.
67	- Commit the record file and its history together.
68	- Write a decision into POSITIONS in the next commit after the curator states it. A proposal of yours enters only at the curator's yes.
69	- The record is public and names models on purpose. Hold nothing back from it for that.
70	
71	## The pass
72	
73	Run the pass when a worker finishes, and before the next boot or batch reads FACTS. In a batch, the commit stage runs it, with this part quoted in its prompt. After a lone worker, you run it.
74	
75	The pass owns each entry's final wording. A rung writes its findings as draft entries: the claim, its conditions, its evidence and what it means.
76	
77	1. Write each new fact as an entry, or rewrite in place the entry that it changes. A rung writes its entries in a file `record.md` in its worktree, and the gather folds them in with `record.py apply`.
78	2. Give each change its provenance: the report section, the commit, and why.
79	3. Check each entry against its source, with bounded `grep`s:
80	   - The cited report section holds what the entry left out.
81	   - The entry keeps the source's scope: the path (walk or the compiled path), the call form (a dotted method call against a top-level call), the range of values and the conditions. Ask: does the entry let a reader conclude more than the evidence shows?
82	   - If a behaviour changed, grep FACTS for it, linked or not. Each entry that states it is updated, or says how it differs.
83	4. Cut any plan or status from each entry (above). If the cut text named a PLAN item or a review-queue item, check that the item names the entry.
84	5. Report each entry over 600 characters, with the question that keeps its extra sentence.
85	
86	Run the same pass on POSITIONS at each landing, and when the curator replaces a decision.
87	
88	## A consolidation
89	
90	A consolidation runs the pass over whole sections. After a batch lands, the record-landing workflow consolidates its entries (`references/batch.md`, "The landing").
91	
92	- In a consolidation, by hand or by the clarity or mining workflow, run a pilot of three or four entries first. Show their new texts to the curator as a page, each with its old text (`SKILL.md`, "Pages"). Run the rest on the curator's go. The pilot shows the curator the form: the length, the register, and what belongs in the history. The other checks, the pass's step 3, the tools' cold readers and the quiz, test only the meaning. The record-landing workflow takes no pilot, since it lands with no step of yours.
93	- Split each section into chunks of 20 to 32 entries.
94	- For each chunk, a Sonnet scout gathers each entry's report sections, its commits and the curator's dated words.
95	- An Opus writer reads this part, the chunk and the scout's file, and writes an apply file. It runs `apply` and `check --base` in its own worktree.
96	- You apply each file on `main`, run `check --base`, commit and push.
97	- Have Opus workers check each new entry by the pass's step 3. Run no Fable review of the entries.
98	- Have a fresh Opus worker answer a small quiz of decisions from the new entries, on the records at hand, without the curator. The decisions must stay as good, and the worker must follow the pointers when needed. If something critical is lost, find the middle ground entry by entry.
99	
100	## The consolidation tools
101	
102	Four Workflow scripts keep the record and the worker skill current and readable. Each one's README says how to run it and what to do with its output. Give a run only its arguments and the input files that its README names. Add no rules of your own over the tool's briefs, and change the briefs only where its README says to, such as their paths. If the briefs do not fit the job, propose their change to the curator. Decide the open questions of the runs as any decision: only a consequential one goes in the review queue.
103	
104	Pick the tool by the job:
105

168	## What the pilot shows about the line between FACTS and its history

170	1. **FACTS says what holds now and what a worker does about it. #!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The record's tool: it owns the form of FACTS.md and POSITIONS.md and of
their two history files, and is the only way to write them.

An entry is one line under a permanent number, `- F-87 **Title.** Text.` in
explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md and `- P-48 **Title.** Text.` in
POSITIONS.md. A number is never reused or changed: a new entry takes the
highest number its file has ever used, plus one. An entry stands under the
nearest `## ` or `### ` heading above it, its section. Its title is its bold
opening, or where it has none, its opening words up to the first colon,
semicolon or full stop.

A pointer is another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, alone
(`It builds P-48.`) or with the first words of the target's title in quotes
(`It builds P-48, "A type parameter the arguments do not fix ..."`, or
`P-48 ("...")`). Quoted words must open the target's current title (`...` or
`…` marks words left out); when an entry is retitled, the tool rewrites them
in every entry that points to it, in the same call.

The history (FACTS-history.md, POSITIONS-history.md beside the record) holds,
under `### F-87`, one block per change, oldest first: one provenance line (the
UTC time from the clock, the kind of change, `from` each report section,
`commit`, `by`, then the note after a colon), and the line as it stood before
the change. The tool derives the kind: `added`, `rewritten`, `moved to "S"`,
`merged into F-n`, `F-n merged in`, `removed`, `noted`; the numbering wrote one
`numbered` block per entry. A retitle that refreshed other entries' pointer
words, or a merge that moved their pointers, says so in one more line of the
block (`pointer words refreshed in: F-12, P-48`).

A `noted` block, which `note` writes, leaves the entry as it is. It adds what
the entry's history lacks, such as the curator's messages behind a text kept
word for word, with their times, or a correction of an earlier block. It holds
no earlier line, and its note says what it adds, so it needs one. A gone entry
takes none: its last block stays `merged into` or `removed`. A noted block
that corrects an earlier block names it by its time, in the field after the
kind: `correcting the block of 2026-10-13 19:07Z`, or, where blocks of the
entry share that minute, `correcting the 2nd block of 2026-10-14 04:41Z`,
counted oldest first. The block corrected is never edited.

Every write takes a lock (flock on .record.lock beside the record), checks the
state it would leave, appends the history blocks first and then replaces each
record file in one step. A write is refused only for what would break the
store: a bad number, a pointer that does not resolve or whose words do not
open its target's title, a line break in an entry, no provenance (neither
`--from` nor `--note`; for a noted block, no `--note`), a correction that
names no block or more than one, two blocks for one entry in one call.
Never for size. The tool does not commit: commit the record file and its
history together.

usage: record.py COMMAND [ARGS] [PROVENANCE] [--root DIR]

  PROVENANCE: --from PATH#HEADING (repeatable; PATH from the repository root
  or from explorations/, HEADING held by exactly one heading of it, as doc:
  resolves one), --commit HASH (in HEAD's history), --by WHO, --note WHY.
  Each write needs --from or --note.

  add F|P --section TITLE FILE   a new entry from FILE's one line, numbered
      record.py add F --section 'Landed semantics' new.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The fix' --by coordinator
  set N [FILE] [--section TITLE] entry N rewritten from FILE's line, or moved
      record.py set F-87 f87.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The question' --note 'cut to the form'
  merge N --into M [FILE]        N removed, M rewritten from FILE (or kept),
                                 every pointer to N made a pointer to M
      record.py merge F-90 --into F-87 f87.md --note 'one fact, two entries'
  remove N                       N removed; refused while a pointer to it remains
      record.py remove P-131 --note 'evicted to the coordinator skill, references/briefing.md'
  note N [--correcting TIME]     a noted block in N's history, N unchanged; needs
                                 --note; refused when the history holds it already.
                                 TIME: 2026-10-13 19:07Z, or 2nd 2026-10-14 04:41Z
      record.py note P-25 --from 'positions-audit/full/evidence/corrections-c1.md#History lines the tool cannot write' --note 'his message behind the text: 2026-09-26T08:01:03.475Z, ...'
      record.py note P-7 --correcting '2026-10-13 19:07Z' --commit b87a17de5 --note 'that block names bc8902f47, ...'
  apply FILE                     many changes from one file, all or none (below)
      record.py apply chunk3.md --by 'consolidation chunk 3'
  check [--base COMMIT]          the store's checks; exit 1 on a failure
      record.py check --base cc9424c2a

An apply file holds, in any order: `## TITLE` or `### TITLE`, the section the
new entries below it go to (an existing entry stands under no heading, or
under its own section's, or the `## ` one that holds it); entry lines as they
should stand, `- F-87 ...`, or `- F-?1 ...` for a new entry, its placeholder
replaced by its number everywhere in the file; `move F-87 to SECTION`;
`remove F-90`; `merge F-91 into F-87`; `note F-87`, or `note F-87 correcting
TIME`, a noted block. Each may be followed by one indented provenance line of
its own:
`  from: PATH, "HEADING"; commit: HASH; by: WHO; note: WHY`. Blank lines and
`<!-- -->` comments are ignored. An entry line equal to the entry is skipped:
to add to its history, write `note F-87`. A note whose block the history holds
already, all but its time, is skipped too, so a file run twice writes nothing
twice. One call writes one block per entry, so an entry is noted, or changed,
once in a file.

check fails on: an entry line without its number, or a line under an entry
that continues it; a number on two lines; a number with no `numbered` or
`added` block, or one gone from its file whose last block is not `merged into`
or `removed`; a noted block that holds an earlier line, or whose `correcting`
names no earlier block of its entry, or more than one; a pointer to no live
entry, or quoted words that do not open the target's title; with --base, an
entry at COMMIT that is neither its line now nor the earlier line of a block
in its history (pointer words refreshed by the tool aside). It reports, without failing: the entries over 600 characters, the
entries without a bold title, and the `--from` paths and the report sections
an entry cites (`PATH`, "HEADING") that do not resolve.

The reads are facts-extract.sh's: `F-87`, `F-87+` (with the entries it points
to and that point to it), `history:F-87`, and the title queries, which fall
back to the former titles in the history.
"""

import collections
import datetime

TREE = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(TOOLS)))   # the checkout this tool is in

1	# The interpreter (walk)
2	
3	Walk's code is in `interpreter/`:
4	
5	- `evaluator/`: the tree walker.
6	- `env/`: the environments, which map names to values, and the wrappers that load components and apis.
7	- `rewrite/`: walk's own rewrite of the tree.
8	- `glue/`: the natives.
9	
10	## How walk evaluates a program
11	
12	After the phases (`SKILL.md`, "The phases"), walk rewrites each component in `interpreter/rewrite/`: it gives each reference to a name the lexical depth of its declaration. The evaluator looks up the name by that depth. The compiled path has no such rewrite.
13	
14	At a call of a generic function, walk infers the static arguments from the run-time types of the arguments (`interpreter/evaluator/EvaluatorBase.java`, `inferAndInstantiateGenericFunction`). Each static parameter gets an interval, from a lower to an upper bound, in a `LatticeIntervalMap` (`useful/`). A type in the domain of an arrow type, such as `T` in `T -> ZZ32`, is contravariant. So its bounds go into the dual map, `LatticeIntervalMapDual`: the same table, with the order reversed. `MakeInferenceSpecific` then makes the inferences more specific, in practice only in the dual map.
15	
16	A generic function passed as a value takes its instance from the arrow type that receives it: a parameter, a local variable declared with the type, or an assignment. So `app(half, v)` runs for `half[\nat n\](x: Vector[\RR64,n\]): Vector[\RR64,n\]` and `app(f: Vector[\RR64,3\] -> Vector[\RR64,3\], v: Vector[\RR64,3\])`. Where no arrow type receives it, or the arrow type leaves a static parameter open, the value stays generic. Walk then infers the static arguments at each application. The checker refuses such a program, so do not rely on this in a program for both paths (ledger row 1021). Walk departs from this in three cases:
17	
18	- An immutable top-level variable of arrow type, an object's field of arrow type and a declared arrow return type keep the generic value. So for a top-level `g: Vector[\RR64,3\] -> Vector[\RR64,3\] = half`, `g(w)` runs for a `w: Vector[\RR64,2\]` (ledger rows 1019, 1036).
19	- For `appT[\T\](f: T -> T, x: T)`, `appT(half, v)` is refused, 'Unification error': `v` fixes `T` by its run-time type. Write the static argument, as `appT(half[\3\], v)` (ledger row 1018).
20	- A generic function declared inside a block stops at its declaration, whether it is passed or not: 'Missing type T' (ledger row 1020). Declare it at the top level.
21	
22	Walk chooses a coercion by the value at run time. The specification and the compiled path choose it statically. Walk has no static types, so it cannot choose statically. The expected-failure tests `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXCoercionStaticRungC.fss` and `XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC.fss` record the difference.
23	
24	Walk departs from the rules of `revival-changes.md`, "Numbers", in these ways, until each fix lands. A test of one of these cases asserts the rules' answer, as an `XXX` test (`tests-writing.md`), unless the case says otherwise.
25	
26	- A `nat` or `int` parameter of 2^31 or more, used as a value, is a `ZZ64` (ledger row 962). Assert no value for it in a test.
27	- A numeral in a call whose other argument is a variable declared `Any` converts by that value's run-time type, not to its default. So `a = 0` is `true` for `a: Any` that holds a zero `NN32`, where the rules' answer is `false` (ledger row 1016). To compare as the rules do, bind the numeral first, as `z = 0`, then write `a = z`.
28	- A numeral with a radix point at a place that fixes no type, which rounds to an infinity at `RR64`, its default, gives `Infinity`, with no error, on both paths (ledger row 980). The rules do not say whether it is an error, so assert no value for it in a test.
29	- A numeral type written as a static parameter's bound or a `typecase` arm's type loads and runs, as in `bnd[\T extends NaturalNumeral[\1, 10, 3\]\](x: ZZ32): ZZ32 = x` (ledger row 1135). The rules refuse it, as the compiled checker does. Walk refuses it at load as a return type, a variable's, a field's or an object's value parameter's type, in an `extends` or `comprises` clause, and as a static argument: 'NaturalNumeral cannot be written in a program except as a parameter's type.'
30	- A body with a declared return type is not converted by coercion, except a numeral: `r(): Wide = NarrowOf(3)` returns the `NarrowOf` (ledger row 387). Write the value at the declared type.
31	
32	Walk also departs from the rules at these bindings:
33	
34	- A `var` declared in a block with an array type and bound to an array literal, as `var t: ZZ32[2] = [5 6]`, is immutable: 'Cannot assign to immutable t' (ledger row 1024). Bind the literal to an immutable name, and initialize the `var` from it.
35	- An array literal assigned to a variable, as `t := [7 8]`, is not built into an array: 'Type mismatch assigning' (ledger row 1025). Bind the literal to an immutable name of the array type, and assign the name.
36	
37	## Where a fix of walk belongs
38	
39	Both paths run the same desugaring phases. Inside them, switches in `Shell.java` decide which desugarings run. Walk turns off these desugarings, which the compiled path runs:
40	
41	- coercion;
42	- chained comparisons;
43	- compound and tuple assignment, and subscripts;
44	- case expressions, typecase and type ascription;
45	- the marking of a bodiless declaration as abstract.
46	
47	Walk evaluates those nodes itself, in `interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java` (`forChainExpr`, `forAssignment`, `forCaseExpr`, `forTypecase`, `forAsExpr`). It converts by coercion at dispatch, in `OverloadedFunction.bestMatchWithCoercion`. So if walk is wrong on one of these nodes, fix the evaluator, not the desugarer.
48	
49	Walk keeps each choice of a declaration in a dispatch cache, except a choice that asked a program's own type for its numeral coercion: that coercion's `where` clause can take one numeral and refuse another. If you change how a numeral chooses a declaration, check that the cache's key (`Numerals.Keys`) tells apart the calls that now choose differently.
50	
51	An edit of a phase that both paths run, or of the desugaring switches, can change both paths. An edit under `interpreter/` changes walk only.
52	
53	## What walk checks
54	
55	Walk does not check static types (`SKILL.md`, "The phases"). The commands that stop after a phase, and `unparse`, use the compiled path's desugaring switches, and the compiler's prelude unless `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one` selects the one library (`compiler.md`, "The `fortress` commands"). So by default `fortress typecheck` does not check a walk program. With the variable, it checks the program against walk's library, but after the compiled path's desugarings. `desugar` or `unparse` does not print the tree that walk runs. That tree is the component's entry in `interpreter_cache/` (`SKILL.md`, "The caches").
56	
57	Under walk, the disambiguator, the phase that binds names, refuses a program's own top-level type that has the name of a type of `FortressLibrary`, such as `Index` or `Indexed`: "Type name may refer to: Index, FortressLibrary.Index". Give such a type another name.
58	
59	At load, walk checks the overload sets, some `comprises` clauses, inherited abstract methods and `override` declarations. It lifts each object expression to the top level as an object, which takes the static parameters of an enclosing generic function, and checks it as an object. It checks a trait or object with static parameters once, through a stand-in: one type for all its instances, with a symbolic type for each static parameter (`symbolicInstance` in `interpreter/evaluator/BuildEnvironments.java`). Through the stand-in, it does not check two functional methods whose parameter types mention a symbolic type. It makes no stand-in, and so checks nothing through one, for a declaration with an `opr` static parameter, or where its static parameters, `where` clause or `extends` clause raise an error at the symbolic types. It refuses:
60	
61	- two declarations of one name that its parameter-by-parameter check cannot order. It accepts them if `comprises` clauses cover the overlap. For every pair of functions of which at least one is generic, it checks the overloading rules of `SKILL.md`, "Fortress as a language", on their declared domains (`revival-changes.md`, "Dispatch and overloading"): the No Duplicates Rule, the Meet Rule and the Return Type Rule. So it refuses two whose declared domains are equal. The message names the rule: "fails because their parameter lists have the same types", "fails the Return Type Rule" or "fails the Meet Rule". Walk keeps the team's check and messages for the pairs below. The team's check looks for a position where the two parameter types neither nest nor exclude. If a parameter type there mentions a static parameter, the message is "at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types". If neither does, it is "are unrelated (neither subtype, excludes, nor equal) and no excluding pair is present". The pairs:
62	  - a pair with a varargs parameter;
63	  - a pair whose parameter lists differ in length, only where one of them has a varargs parameter. Walk checks no other pair of lists of different lengths;
64	  - a pair that is neither two generic declarations, nor a generic one beside a plain one, nor a generic function beside a generic trait's or object's functional method that has no static parameters of its own;
65	  - the instances of an explicit instantiation.
66	
67	  Where it reads exclusion over the whole tuple of parameter types, at the instance that the equalities force, it reads two parameter types that still mention a static parameter as excluding only where no instances of the two can meet. Walk departs from the rules in these cases:
68	  - At load, it does not check two functional methods of a generic trait or object on their declared domains. It compares them at each call, on the instance that the call makes. So where the two declared domains lie one inside the other, a valid pair stops the run when the program first makes the extending object at its static arguments, as `H[\ZZ32\]()` for `object H[\S\]() extends Holds[\S\]`: 'at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types' (ledger row 780).
69	  - It refuses two generic functional methods whose declared domains lie one inside the other, in a type without static parameters (ledger row 779).
70	  - It refuses a pair whose overlap it finds only through an instance of a supertype, also where a third declaration covers the overlap (ledger row 539).
71	  - It refuses overloads on two instantiations of one generic type, as `g(b: Tg[\3\])` beside `g(b: Tg[\4\])` (ledger row 416).
72	  - Its parameter-by-parameter check reads an object type over a static parameter as excluding a type that one of its instances is or extends. So it loads `g[\T\](x: Box[\T\], y: ZZ32)` beside `g(x: Box[\ZZ32\], y: Any)`, which the Meet Rule refuses (ledger row 788).
73	  - It reads no `where` clause when it reads exclusion over the whole tuple. So it refuses such a pair where one declaration has a `where` clause of its own (ledger row 787).
74	  - It does not refuse a type that extends a self-typed trait `T[\A\]` and is not an `A` (`revival-changes.md`, "Traits and objects"). A call that both `T`'s operator and another declaration fit then runs one of them, without an ambiguity error (ledger row 893). Make each type that extends `T[\A\]` an `A`.
75	  - It loads a generic top-level function whose declared domain lies inside that of a self-typed trait's functional method of the same name, where the Return Type Rule holds. The checker refuses every top-level function more specific than a functional method of its name, a check that the specification does not state: '… is more specific than the declaration of the functional method' (ledger row 894).
76	  - It loads a function over `Index` beside one over a pair whose element types neither lie below `Index` nor exclude it, which the Meet Rule refuses (ledger row 806).
77	  - It loads a type that provides two functional symbolic operators, such as two `||`, that break the Meet Rule for Functional Methods (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`). The checker refuses the pair (ledger row 611).
78	  - Beside a generic declaration, it does not judge by the Return Type Rule a declaration without static parameters that writes no return type and whose parameter types are object types, as the number types other than `QQ` are: `pick[\T extends Number\](a: T): ZZ32 = 1` beside `pick(a: NN32) = "two"` loads (ledger row 1044). Write the return type.
79	  - It reads no `comprises` clause for the Return Type Rule. So it refuses a valid pair over a program's own trait that comprises one object, as `pickFirst[\T extends Number\](a: T, b: T): T` beside `pickFirst(a: Mine, b: Mine): Mine`, where `Mine` extends `Number` and comprises one object.
80	  - It reads two parameter lists as excluding where, in one of them, every parameter at which the two differ is an object type, even an object below the other list's type there. So `f(x: Number): ZZ32` beside `f(x: ZZ64): String` loads, which the checker refuses (ledger row 697).

82	
83	  The paths differ on `f[\T extends { K, R[\T\] }\](x: T)` beside `f(x: Z)`, where `K comprises { A, B, C }`, `Z excludes { A, B }`, and `C` is an object that extends `Z` but not `R`. 90	  - an object expression, which takes its static parameters from the function around it;

111	## Natives
112	
113	The library binds each of walk's natives by a declaration whose body is `builtinPrimitive("…")`. The string names one of these:

17	## What the two paths share
18	
19	After the phases, each path has its own code for these:

21	- Values: walk's `interpreter/evaluator/values/` (`FInt`, `FFloat`), and the compiled `compiler/runtimeValues/` (`FZZ32`, `FRR64`), payload classes, which hold the JVM value, as `FRR64` holds a `double`. 24	- The run: `fortress run` starts a second JVM (`bin/run`), which never enters `Shell.java`.

26	Both paths run the helpers, the public static methods of classes under `nativeHelpers/`.

30	## The compiler's prelude, until the switch-over
31	
32	The compiled path uses the compiler's own prelude: `LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss`, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss` and `Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss`. With `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`, it uses the one library in their place. The runtime's classes that name a library's types, as `FValue`, `FException` and `LibraryNames`, come in two sets under the same names: one built from `ProjectFortress/src` into `ProjectFortress/build`, for the prelude, and one built from `ProjectFortress/src-one` into `ProjectFortress/build-one`, for the one library. `ant compileAll` builds both. With the variable, the class path puts the second set first. If you change a class that `src-one` also holds, make the same change to its copy there. `LibraryNames` gives the JVM names of its library's classes, as the class of an exception that a helper raises by its simple name. `Library/CompilerSystem.fss` is the compiled path's `System`.

41	- an object expression;
42	- an array literal, such as `[1 2 3]`;

90	## What the code generator does
91	
92	- It emits no primitive `double` arithmetic.
93	- It runs a program's own `coerce` from a numeral once for each place where the numeral is written, in the component class's static initializer, except where the place's type names a type parameter (below). The runtime initializes the class of each component that the program's classes name before `run()`, in one task. So a coercion's output comes before the program's first line, and the parallel parts of a coercion's body run one after another there. A coercion that raises stops the program before `run()`. A test of a coercion that raises sets `run_exits_nonzero=true` (`tests-writing.md`).
94	- The class loader rewrites a template's bytes with ASM. The emitted classfiles stay at version 1.6, because this rewriting keeps no stack-map frames. Do not raise the version.
95	- The `value` modifier adds the mark interface `ValueObjectMark` to the object's class. The compiled `SEQV` (`nativeHelpers/equality.java`) reads the mark. The modifier does not inline or unbox the fields.
96	- An array of `RR64` values is to be stored as an unboxed `double[]`. The code generator does not build it yet. If your task touches how arrays are stored, print the two POSITIONS entries on arrays first (about 2 KB):

100	## The runtime
101	
102	- The class loader is `runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java`. The revival has changed it for sizes, for the lock on a class's first load (ledger row 417), and to choose a call's opcode from the class file of the called method's class, without loading that class. Before you investigate a failure while a class loads, read ledger rows 408 and 559, which name it (`records.md`, "Reading the record").
103	- The compiled code keeps each mutable variable in a cell (`compiler/runtimeValues/MutableFValue.java`), and an object's `var` field in a cell that the object holds. Before each read and write of the cell, the generated code asks `BaseTask.inATransaction()` (`runtimeSystem/`). Inside an `atomic` block, the access goes through the transaction. So the transaction tracks the variables that the block touches. From the switch-over, it also tracks each element of the one library's arrays, by array and index: `compiler/runtimeValues/FortressArrayStore.java` calls the transaction's methods `TXReadSlot` and `TXWriteSlot`. Walk does not run this class, so test an edit of it with `ArrayStoreJUTest`, beside it.

105	## Natives
106	
107	`import java com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.{...}` in a `.fss` file binds static Java methods over plain Java values.
108	
109	A body `builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.Class.method")` binds one such method, a helper, too. In a compile, at the parse, the compiled path, and not walk, rewrites the body as a call of the method through a generated `import java`, with `self` first in a trait or object (`compiler/BuiltinPrimitiveRewriter.java`). The checker then checks the declaration against the method's Java signature. In a compile, it reads `int` as `ZZ32`, `long` as `ZZ64`, `float` as `RR32`, `double` as `RR64`, `boolean` as `Boolean`, `String` as `JavaString`, `BigInteger` as `ZZ` and `Object` as `Any` (`NamingCzar.fortressTypeForForeignJavaType`). The compile stops in these cases:
110	
111	- If the string is in that package but names no public static method: 'builtinPrimitive names no static helper: …'.
112	- If the string names a glue class or anything else outside that package: 'Variable builtinPrimitive is not defined.'
113	- If the declaration has a varargs parameter: the same message (ledger row 849).
114	- If the declaration is a local function or a method of an object expression: the same message. The rewrite reaches only a component's declarations and the members of its traits and objects (ledger row 865).

116	The rewrite runs only in a JVM that has made a Fortress repository of the compiled path, the compiler's store of components, not this git repository. Walk's repository switches it off again. `fortress compile` makes one, and so do `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` and `typecheck` (`Shell.compilerPhases`). `fortress parse` and `fortress api` make none, so they rewrite a body only after a compile in the same JVM (ledger row 882). Alone, they pass a misspelt helper. Test a binding with `compile`. In a suite, the result of `parse` or `api` depends on whether a compile ran earlier in the same JVM.

131	## Traps of the compiled path
132	
133	- The compiler's prelude declares `print`, `println` and `String`'s `||` at `Object`, not `Any` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:37`, `:55`, `:61`). So until the switch-over, the checker refuses a generic that prints a value of a type parameter written without a bound, or concatenates it onto a `String`. The message names `Object`, as 'Object->() is not applicable to an argument of type T.' does for `println`. In such a generic of a compiled program or test, write `T extends Object`. The generic then takes no tuple, function or `()`. The one library declares these operations at `Any` or `String`, so do not change its text for this limit. The prelude's `||` takes the string first only, so `c || s` for a `Character` value `c` is refused (ledger row 965). Put a string first, as `("" || c) || s`.
134	- Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude declares no `=/=` at `RR32` and `RR64`, so the checker refuses `r =/= 0` for an `RR64` value `r` (ledger row 1059). Write `NOT (r = 0)`. For an `RR32` value `c`, the checker refuses `c = 0`: 'Ambiguous coercion in call to operator ='. `c = d` for two `RR32` values compiles, and overflows the stack when it runs (ledger row 528). Bind `c` at `RR64` first, as `r: RR64 = c`, and compare `r`.
135	- A parameter of a declared tuple type is one JVM parameter for each element (F-378). So in a `VerifyError`, the method's descriptor lists each element of a tuple parameter as a parameter of its own. These three tuple forms fail:
136	  - an object's method overloaded at a pair and at another type fails the JVM's verification (ledger row 1054). Give the two methods two names;
137	  - an object whose one value parameter is a pair dies in its constructor with `ClassCastException` (ledger row 1055). Add a second value parameter beside the pair, as `object Holder(n: ZZ32, var pr: (ZZ32, ZZ32))`;
138	  - a generic operator whose one parameter has its type parameter's type, applied to a pair, dies at the call with `NoSuchMethodError`, as `pr!!` for `opr (x: T)!![\T\] : T = x` and `pr = (1, 2)` (ledger row 1056). Write no such call in a compiled program.
139	- A `try`'s `forbid` clause lists exception types: an exception of a listed type that no `catch` clause took is wrapped in a `ForbiddenException`, which the `try` throws. A `try`'s `finally` clause does not run when one of these leaves the `try` block: an `exit`, an exception that no `catch` clause takes, or the `ForbiddenException` that the `try` throws (ledger row 890). So write no compiled program that relies on `finally` after an exception or an `exit` leaves the `try`. A test that needs it is an `XXX` test (`tests-writing.md`). A `try` whose block can throw, with a `finally` clause and no `catch` or `forbid` clause, fails with a `VerifyError` at class load (ledger row 891).
140	- To fork is to run as tasks that can run at once. A call's arguments and an operator's operands fork, as the rule says, where two or more of them are calls, written `f(x)`, of functions that the program declares. So write no compiled program that relies on the order in which its arguments are evaluated. Until the switch-over, the calls written in the compiler's prelude do not fork, so a compiled `SUM` runs one body at a time (ledger row 982). A compiled parallel `for` runs its bodies at once: use it in a test of parallelism.

So does a `try` as an operator's operand after the first (ledger row 526). Bind its value in a statement of its own.
142	- Numerals and sizes depart from `revival-changes.md`, "Numbers", in these ways:

Test which exception was raised by the type of the `catch` clause that takes it.
154	- A reference to a generic function with one declaration, as `count[\F extends Object\](b: Box[\F\]): ZZ32`, takes its instance from the arrow type that receives it. 170	## The checker's gaps
171	
172	- Overloads: in its test of whether two domains exclude each other, the checker puts the meet of a static parameter's declared bounds in the parameter's place where the parameter is a whole parameter type, an element of a tuple or a member of an intersection or union (P-157). Inside a static argument, as `T` in `Box[\T\]`, the parameter stays. The paths differ on `tint[\T extends Red\](x: Box[\T\])` beside `tint[\T extends Blue\](x: Box[\T\])`, where `Red`, `Blue` and `Box` are objects. The checker refuses it, because `Box[\Bottom\]` lies in both domains, and walk loads it. No decision says which is right. Assert neither path's answer in a test (ledger row 786).
173	- The Return Type Rule: the checker refuses a pair of declarations that the rule accepts: a generic declaration beside one without static parameters whose domain is a tuple of object types, as `ident[\T\](x: T): T` beside `ident(x: (Circle, Circle)): (Circle, Circle)`, `Circle` an object (ledger row 1048). Walk loads and runs the pair. The checker also applies the rule where a type redeclares an inherited getter, with each getter's receiver read as the type that declares it. In an object expression, it checks no getter or dotted method against the inherited one, so `fortress typecheck` accepts a pair there that breaks the rule (ledger row 1097). Check such a pair against the rule yourself. The checker refuses a narrower return type where an object redeclares an abstract dotted method of a self-typed trait at the same parameter types (ledger row 1094; `revival-changes.md`, "Traits and objects").
174	- A method call through a type variable whose bound is another type variable: the checker refuses `x.n()` with `x: F` in `chained[\H extends Gen, F extends H\]`, where the trait `Gen` declares `n()`: 'No such method F.n.'. Walk runs the call (ledger row 1093). Write `F extends Gen` in place of `F extends H`.
175	- Inheritance: the checker refuses an object that reaches a generic self-typed trait's method along two paths, one through a trait that declares the method again at the same parameter types: 'There are multiple declarations of m with the same parameter type'. Without static parameters it accepts the form. Walk runs the lower trait's declaration. The specification's section "Method Declarations" (`Specification/basic/traits.tex`) does not settle which is right. Assert neither path's answer in a test (ledger row 1037).
176	- A `where` clause's constraint: the checker checks a function's or functional method's constraint on its own static parameters at the call. At a dotted call, a candidate is not applicable where the receiver's static argument breaks the method's constraint. A trait's or object's own constraint is checked where its type is used, also at a constructor call; only the checker reads it, and the compiled code does not check it. A `where`-clause variable is a static parameter of the function's arrow type, inferred at the call. The checker does not yet check these, and no ledger row holds the first two:
177	  - at a dotted call, a constraint whose bound names the method's own static parameters or a `where`-clause variable;
178	  - at a type's use, a constraint whose bound names a `where`-clause variable;
179	  - a static argument written at a top-level call, against its parameter's bound (ledger row 470).
180	- A reduction without its static argument, whose bound names its parameter, such as `SUM`: the checker reports a type error in its body as the big operator's refusal, 'is not applicable to an argument of type ()' (ledger row 1015). Write the static argument to read the body's error.
181	- Imports: `import A.{...}`, with the three dots written, imports every name of `A`. The overloading check also reads `A`'s declarations of a name that the component imports by name from another api. So `import A.{...}` beside `import B.{ pick }`, where both apis declare `pick(x: P)`, is refused: 'There are multiple declarations of pick' (ledger row 813). Leave the name out of the whole import, as `import A.{...} except { pick }`.
182	- An `except` clause leaves out each identifier that it lists, on both paths. Neither path leaves out an infix operator that it lists. So where a component lists `-` in `except` and declares its own `-` at the api's parameter types, the code generator stops. Walk runs the component's own `-` (ledger row 814).
183	- Conditional extension: the condition holds while the checker checks the `extends` entry itself, an object's value parameters and every member. It does not hold for the other `extends` entries, the static parameters, the declaration's own `where` clause, and the `excludes` and `comprises` clauses. The checker lets a member that it checked under the condition be called where the condition fails (ledger row 773).
184	- A `comprises` clause that lists a type at a `where`-clause variable, as `NatParam comprises { N[\n\] } where [\ nat n \]` or `AnyList comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]`: at a call, the checker gives the variable a fresh size or type, equal only to itself. Two values passed in one call get two. A fresh type is bounded by the binding and by the clause's constraints. The variable is in scope in the trait, except in its `extends` and `excludes` clauses. The checker gives no fresh type where it meets the trait as a supertype of another type. Where the variable is a size, a compiled call that passes a value of such a trait where a listed type is expected fails the JVM's verification (ledger row 307). Departures: a fresh type also under a function type's result (ledger row 751), none for an extender that the clause does not list (ledger row 752), and a crash at a call, from outside the trait, of a member whose type names the variable (ledger row 756).
185	
186	## The `fortress` commands
187	
188	`Shell.java` dispatches `bin/fortress <command>`.
189	
190	- To see what an early phase makes of a program, stop after that phase: `parse` (a syntax check), `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` or `typecheck`.
191	- `unparse` prints the syntax tree back as Fortress source. Use it to see what a desugaring made.
192	- `link` links a compiled component (the `link` step of a compiled `.test` file). `api` writes a component's api. `test` runs a program's `test` declarations under walk.
193	- The command chooses the library. Walk and `test` call `Shell.useInterpreterLibraries()`. Every other command calls `useCompilerLibraries()`. Each call points `WellKnownNames` and `Types` to its prelude, and sets the desugaring switches. With `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`, `useCompilerLibraries()` points them to the one library (`Shell.java:377-388`).
194	
195	## Running
196	
197	    cd ProjectFortress
198	    # after an ant compileAll that started the caches again: the library order (build-and-caches.md)
199	    ../bin/fortress compile <path>/P.fss
200	    ../bin/fortress run P [args]
201	
202	A small program compiles in about 5 s and runs in about 1 s.
203	
204	- A crash of the checker prints one line and hides the Java stack. To see the stack, put `-debug stacktrace` before the file: `../bin/fortress compile -debug stacktrace <path>/P.fss`.
205	- A failed compile of a program leaves a 0-byte jar in `bytecode_cache/`. A run of the program then prints "Could not load P" and "Resource not found". Read the compile's error instead.
206	
207	## Before an edit
208	
209	Two notes under `explorations/coordinator/map/` help you find where a fix belongs. A status or a line number in them can be stale. Before you rely on a status, read the ledger rows that it cites. Before you rely on a line number, grep for the method's name.
210	
211	- Before you add or fix a language feature, print its row of the feature table. WORD names the feature, such as `spawn`, `coercion` or `typecase`. A row is about 1 KB. It names the feature's section of the specification, its parser rule, checker class, walk site, code-generator site, prelude declaration and ledger rows.
212	
213	      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:spec-to-implementation.md#Feature by feature@WORD'
214	
215	- If your edit is in one phase, and you need what runs before and after it on each path, print that phase's section. Name the section by its number and the first word of its title. A section is 1 to 3 KB. B.1 is the phase list, B.4 disambiguation, B.5 desugaring, B.6 type checking, B.7 overloading, B.10 the caches, B.11 the runtime and B.12 the natives.
216	
217	      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:modules-and-phases.md#B.5 Desugaring'
218	
219	- Before you change the text of a diagnostic, grep the `.test` files for it. A `.test` file can pin a whole diagnostic with `compile_err_equals`, its `file:line:column` included. `grep -l 'TEXT' ProjectFortress/*tests/*.test`, with words of the diagnostic as TEXT, lists the files that pin it. Update each of those in the same commit. A line that you add to or remove from a compiler test program moves the pinned spans below it.
220	
221	## Testing an edit here
222	
223	- For a quick loop on an edit of the checker or the code generator, compile the edited class into a scratch directory, and run the compiler with that directory first on its class path. Give each run a fresh copy of the caches, because nothing checks the caches against the compiler that wrote them, and a compile of an unchanged program with a jar writes nothing:
224	
225	      Q=$PWD/tmp/quick ; export FORTRESS_CACHES=$Q/caches ; CP=$(bin/fortress_classpath | tail -1)
226	      mkdir -p $Q/classes && javac -nowarn -cp "$CP" -d $Q/classes ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/<path>/X.java
227	      rm -rf $Q/caches && cp -a default_repository/caches $Q/caches
228	      java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -Dfortress.caches=$Q/caches -cp "$Q/classes:$CP" com.sun.fortress.Shell compile P.fss
229	      bin/fortress run P
230	
231	  For a Scala file, compile it with `java -cp "$CP" scala.tools.nsc.Main -classpath "$CP" -d $Q/classes -encoding UTF-8 X.scala`. Then put the edit into the tree and build it for real.
232	- If your change is near transactions, top-level mutable state or the class loader's first load, do the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`).
233	
234	## The checker's time
235	
236	This section is for a change of the checker: its Scala under `scala_src/`, or `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast` and the generators under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/`, from which the build generates the checker's syntax tree and `Walker`.
237	
238	The count stage takes `<out-file> <scratch>` and about 80 to 180 seconds, more under load. It can run past the Bash tool's 120-second limit, so run it in the background (`session.md`). It writes a table to the out-file: the errors of each api, the total, the number of places with errors, and the first crash. It keeps the checker's whole output in `<scratch>/run.txt`, and its caches in `<scratch>`, so a run from the base build leaves the base build as it was.
239	
240	The checker checks every api first, and the component only if no api has an error. In each api or component, it stops at the first of its stages that finds errors. The stages run in this order (`compiler/StaticChecker.java`, `checkCompilationUnit`):
241	
242	1. The type hierarchy and the type check.
243	2. The overloading check, which also compares the overloads' return types.
244	3. In the component only, the export check (`library.md`, "Designing a change").
245	
246	So the count misses the errors of the later stages, and a fix of an early error can raise it.
247	
248	The table's rows tell a clean run from a run that the checker did not finish:
249	
250	- `#total 0` and `#locations 0`: the checker reached the component and found no error.
251	- `#stopped`, in place of `#total` and `#locations`: the errors came from a phase before the checker, such as the parse. The checker reported none and did not reach the component. The script exits 1, and the gate reads the table as red.
252	- `#crash`: the first crash of the overloading check that the run survived, or `none`.
253	
254	If the run printed no error total and was not clean, the script writes no table and exits 1.
255	
256	The checker's results are the programs that it accepts and refuses, and each error with its text and its place. On the interpreter's library, a change keeps the results the same if both of these hold:
257	
258	- The two tables are equal: `diff` prints nothing.
259	- The two `run.txt` files are equal after you replace each run's own tree path with one word, such as `TREE`. Any difference fails.
260	
261	A node's hash starts from its class name, so an order in the output, such as the apis' checks, does not vary from run to run. A moved order is a difference: keep the old order, or report it.
262	
263	`Walker`, in the generated `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/nodes/FortressAst.scala`, is split into methods under 8,000 bytes of bytecode. HotSpot does not compile a longer method, and the walker runs on every node. `MethodSizeJUTest` fails if a method of the build grows past the limit, except the methods that its source lists in `listed(...)` entries. Run it alone with `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=MethodSizeJUTest`. If a method of `Walker` fails, lower `WALKER_CASES_PER_METHOD` in `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/ScalaAstGenerator.java`. If another method fails, split it under the limit. List it only if nothing in the checker or a compiled run calls it, with its size and what runs it, and name it in your report.
264	
265	The timing is a smoke test, to catch a slowdown of several times. One run of each tree is enough. A small difference, or one within the noise from run to run, is not a finding. In your report, say what you saw, and do not analyse it.
266	
267	If you change the checker:
268	
269	1. Make the change correct, with its tests. Commit it, and name the commit in your report.
270	2. Time the base build and the change, named `base` and `change`. Run the base in a call set up for the base build (`build-and-caches.md`), and the change in a call set up for your tree, each in the background (`session.md`). Use the same command for both, with `N` the run's name:
271	
272	       export W=<your tree> N=base ; mkdir -p $W/tmp/count
273	       time explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh $W/tmp/count/$N.txt $W/tmp/count/$N
274	
275	3. Make a second pass that makes the checker faster. Start with a profile (below). Where the profile shows a gain, take it. Where it shows none, say so in your report, with the profile's top frames.
276	4. If the second pass changed code, run the count stage once more with the command of step 2, named `pass`. Show that its results are the same as `change`'s. Then run `ant testQuick` once more (`tests-running.md`, "When to run a whole suite"). If it changed nothing, run neither, and report `change`'s results in place of `pass`'s.
277	5. If the pass reuses an answer that the checker computed earlier, as a memo does, audit it on one full run. Put the audit in an instrumented copy ("Testing an edit here"), never in the tree. In the audit, compute each reused answer again and compare the two. If any answer differs, the reuse is wrong: fix it or drop it, then repeat step 4. Report the count of reuses and of differences.
278	6. In your report, give each run's seconds, the diff of the `base` and `change` tables, the comparison of their `run.txt` files, and that `pass` has the same results as `change`.
279	
280	To find where the time goes, use JFR on the count stage's checker, instrumented copies compiled into a scratch folder ahead of the build on the class path, and the methods over 8,000 bytes that `MethodSizeJUTest` lists in its source. A profiled or instrumented run is neither a timed run nor a run to compare. Print the commands of two earlier speed probes (about 8 KB):
281	
282	    explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/perf-probes/checker-speed-2/REPORT.md#Decisions, findings' 'doc:explorations/perf-probes/checker-speed/REPORT.md#Decisions, findings'
283	
284	If your brief asks you to review a change of the checker, run the count stage yourself. Time the base build and the worker's commit of step 1 once each, as step 2 says, with the commit and the worker's head in worktrees seeded at them (`worktrees.md`). Check that your times are the worker's, in order of size. Check that the commit's and the head's results are the same.
285

6:**library order**
59:- A `.fss` or `.fsi` file of the library: the entries of that component, and after an `.fsi` edit, the entries of every component that imports the api. Walk analyses them again by itself. A component of the compiler's library needs a compile, or the library order ("After an edit of the library").
71:Only these runs read `default_repository/caches`: `fortress compile`, `fortress run`, `fortress junit` (and `junit.sh`), `ant testOnly`, and a direct walk run. These runs use private caches (`-Dfortress.caches` and `FORTRESS_CACHES`), and need neither the library order nor warm caches: `harness-one.sh`, the gate's step 7 (`gate.md`) and both ant suites. `harness-one.sh` keeps its private cache beside its scratch folder between calls (`tests-running.md`).
73:With `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`, a run that names no private caches folder uses `default_repository/caches-one` in place of `default_repository/caches`, because a caches folder holds the jars of a single library. Set the environment variable, not only the property `-Dfortress.library=one`. The class path scripts, `bin/fortress_classpath` and `bin/run_classpath`, read only the variable. With the property alone, the compile writes to `caches-one`, but the run looks in `caches` and prints 'Could not load P'. Run the library order without the variable: it fills `caches` with the prelude's jars. A program compiled with the variable runs only if its caches folder holds the jars of the one library's fourteen components, which `one_library_tests/OneLibraryComponents.test` compiles. To fill `caches-one` with them, run that test with `junit.sh` and the variable (`tests-running.md`, "Compiled tests").
75:## The library order
84:Otherwise the jars are in place, and a compiled test or program needs no library order. The five commands:
93:Before the first compiled run, check that `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/` holds five jars: `fortress.AnyType.jar`, `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`, `fortress.CompilerLibrary.jar`, `fortress.CompilerAlgebra.jar` and `CompilerSystem.jar`, which has no prefix. Sometimes all five compiles exit 0 and a jar is missing. The cause is not known.
116:- After a build that started the caches again, yours or a test target's, run the library order before the next compiled run. So each edit of Java or Scala costs about 2 to 3 minutes before a compiled run: the build, then the library order.
124:- If you edited the `.fsi` of AnyType, CompilerBuiltin, CompilerLibrary or CompilerAlgebra: run the whole library order. Every api depends on these four.
135:If you see either, do the step now: recompile the component, or run the library order. Do not delete the caches to fix it. A deletion works only because it repeats the library order and every analysis from cold. If something else looks like a stale cache, find its cause before you delete anything.

content.content:
- P-12 **After the switch-over, walk runs the compiled type checker on its programs, and then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts.** The curator wants the checker usable on the programs that walk runs. Today `fortress typecheck` checks a program against the compiler's prelude unless `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one` selects the one library, so by default it is no check of walk's programs (F-9 holds this fact). Walk is not changed for this before the switch-over. After it, walk runs the checker on its programs and so gains their static types; F-9 and F-290 say what walk and the library lack for that step. Walk then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts, in place of its choice on the run-time value (P-59, walk's choice of coercions until the switch-over).

- P-17 **Unboxed doubles and arrays of unboxed doubles are required: without them the revival misses its point.** Why: a language meant for high performance cannot box its numbers. Today the code generator boxes every number: an `RR64` value is an object of the class `FRR64`. In Java models of microGPT's three array kernels, the dot product, the matrix product and the row lift, boxing is the main cost (F-11 holds the measurement). How arrays store doubles, as `double[]`, is P-84's decision.

- P-45 **Overloaded declarations may differ in their static parameters.** The specification drops its sentence that forbids this, and keeps it as superseded text. It states instead the overloading model of the type group's 2011 paper (`Papers/Types/`), which the compiled checker already used. The checker keeps the paper's three rules: No Duplicates, Meet and Return Type. It checks the Return Type Rule over every instance of a generic declaration that the argument types allow, not over one guessed instance. One rule of the old sentence survives: if one generic declaration is more specific than another, their static parameters must line up position by position, as Java's rule for overriding a generic method requires. The compiled checker tests it only where the two declarations have as many static parameters of their own (F-75). Walk chooses among overloads by the parameter types that each declaration declares, not by the order in which they are written. At load, walk judges each pair of two generic declarations by the checker's rules on their declared parameter types. It does not refuse a pair only because none of their parameter types exclude, as when one declaration is more specific than the other. Walk and the checker must accept the same pairs. The library repairs, by declarations of its own, the overload sets that the checker refused, and no line of microGPT's two programs changes. Where walk or the checker still judges a pair against these rules: walk compares two functional methods of a generic trait or object on the instance that a call makes (F-26); both paths refuse the paper's own valid example (row 539); walk refuses two generic functional methods of a trait without static parameters whose declared domains lie one inside the other, and stops at an extending o

- P-84 **On the compiled path, the array of every number type is to be stored unboxed, in a Java array of its primitive type, and every array is to have the most efficient store that its element type allows; arrays keep the team's `nat` sizes in their types.** `RR64` goes in a `double[]`, `ZZ32` in an `int[]`, and so on, for each number type that has a Java primitive type; `RR64`'s `double[]`, the model's, is the first case. Why: a high-performance language cannot box its array elements, and the sizes are central to the team's design. So the storage and the sizes are one design: the sizes stay in the array types as `nat` static parameters, as the library's `Vector` and `Matrix` declare them, and the compiled checker checks them. The sizes do not wait while a first version of the store carries them only as run-time fields; that layered plan was rejected.
