content.content:
## The library order

The first of its compiles, `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, holds the top type `Any`, which both libraries share. The other four are the compiler's own. All five take about 100 to 110 s after `ant compileAll`.

Run it only when the caches lack the library's jars, or hold stale ones:

- after a build that printed `Caches <tree>/default_repository/caches started again, empty`, and in a tree whose caches are empty;
- after an edit of a library `.fsi` that the section "After an edit of the library" names.

Otherwise the jars are in place, and a compiled test or program needs no library order. The five commands:

    cd ProjectFortress
    ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss            # 17 s
    ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss    # 63 s
    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerLibrary.fss        # 27 s
    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss        # 2 s
    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerSystem.fss         # 2 s

Before the first compiled run, check that `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/` holds five jars: `fortress.AnyType.jar`, `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`, `fortress.CompilerLibrary.jar`, `fortress.CompilerAlgebra.jar` and `CompilerSystem.jar`, which has no prefix. Sometimes all five compiles exit 0 and a jar is missing. The cause is not known.

- If a jar is missing, run the five commands again. Once, this made the jars.

- F-405 **Walk runs the generic dotted methods of one name that a trait or an object declares together, each as its instance at symbolic static arguments.** An object takes each generic method of a name, alone or beside others of the name, with one symbolic instantiation for each name and, per static parameter, kind and bounds, with the method's own static parameters in the bounds compared by position, not by name (`interpreter/evaluator/values/Constructor.java`, `genericKey`): so an object's redeclaration of a trait's generic method at the same bounds under other names hides it, and two that differ in their bounds are overloads, except bounds that differ only in the api of a type of one simple name (row 1134). At load walk reads two such instances on their declared domains where one lies inside the other; a set of them whose overlap only a third covers is refused (row 1133), and so is, when an extending object's first instance is made, a nested pair of a generic trait's generic functional methods (row 780). An object that inherits two such methods of one name from two traits, neither more specific, with no declaration at their meet, loads and runs, where the Meet Rule refuses the set (row 1139). A call that writes no static argument infers them and dispatches among the instances, the inner declared domain first; a call that writes static arguments instantiates each generic method whose static parameters, by their number and kinds, take them, and chooses among those instances
- F-253 **Under walk, a call of a generic method that writes no static argument infers the method's own static arguments from the arguments' run-time types.** This holds for a dotted call, as for a call of a generic function, whether the method is alone under its name or among its receiver's overloads. Among the receiver's overloads, where one of two is a generic dotted method and exactly one of their declared domains lies inside the other, walk chooses the inner one, except for two generic dotted methods whose bounds differ only in the api of a type of one simple name, of which the object's is kept (row 1134, F-405); otherwise it compares them on the instance that the call makes (F-252). A generic method that a trait declares reads its bounds, and the types to which its arguments convert, in the trait's method environment, where its instances bind and evaluate their types, as a method that an object declares does. So it takes the instance that the same method declared in an object takes: a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` give `Box[\ZZ64\]` with the `ZZ32` converted, and a bounded type parameter that nothing fixes takes its bound. ## 1. The answer

One training step is the forward pass, the backward pass and the Adam update, for one document (batch 1), in 64-bit floats, at n_embd 16, block 16, 4 heads, 1 layer, vocabulary 27, 4,192 parameters. All five lines were measured on 2026-11-10 between 14:36 and 14:46 UTC on this machine, one program after another, with another worker's builds and runs beside them (load 1.6 to 5.4 on 4 CPUs). Section

    program                                  seconds per step   what the time includes
    pure Java (flat layout)                  0.000113           step + Adam, 16 padded positions; after 4 s of warm-up
    NumPy (flat layout, microgpt_flat.py)    0.000201           step + Adam, 16 padded positions; after 500 steps
    dzaima/APL (flat layout)                 0.0130             step + Adam, 16 padded positions; after 500 steps
    dzaima/APL (object layout, microgpt.apl) 0.0077             step + Adam, the document's own positions (mean 7.2); after 500 steps
    pure Python (Karpathy's microgpt.py)     0.132              step + Adam, the document's own positions (mean 7.3); after 20 steps

Ratios, from the medians:

- NumPy / Java = 1.8. Java is the faster one.
- dzaima flat / Java = 115; dzaima flat / NumPy = 65.
- pure Python / Java = 1,180 as each program runs. The pure Python program does less work in a step: it computes only the document's positions, 7.3 on average, where the flat programs compute 16. Per position, pure Python takes 18.2 ms and Java 0.0070 ms: 2,600 times.
- pure Python / NumPy = 660 per step as each runs; pure Python / dzaima flat = 10.

Which comparisons are of one session: all of them. The Python, NumPy and dzaima runs were interleaved in five rounds, and the Java bench ran between rounds 3 and 4. The Java number is from the Java worker's program as it stood uncommitted at 14:42; `java-baseline/REPORT.md` did not exist when this note was written, after 24 minutes of polling, so the Java worker's own timings are not compared here

**His expectation.** "Java faster than pure Python": holds, by three orders of magnitude. "Java slower than NumPy": does not hold at this size. Java is 1.8 times faster at batch 1, and about level at batch 4 (Java 404 µs, NumPy 414 µs for the step alone).

**The reason, by reading.** At widths of 16 the step is about 200,000 multiply-adds: the forward products are about 64,000 (three 16×16 by 16×16 for Q, K, V; 4 heads of 16×4 by 4×16 and 16×16 by 16×4; one 16×16; two between 16 and 64 wide; one to 27 wide), and each has two products in the backward pass.

- *Java* does that arithmetic and little else. 0.113 ms for 200,000 multiply-adds is about 1.8 billion a second, the rate of scalar double arithmetic on one core of this machine. Its step is bound by arithmetic.
- *NumPy* makes 190 function calls per step, counted by `cProfile`, 29 of them matrix products. On this machine a 16×16 by 16×16 product costs 0.80 µs, `x*x` on 16×16 0.33 µs, `np.sqrt` 0.46 µs, and a `mean(-1, keepdims=True)` 2.3 µs; the arithmetic inside a 16×16 product is 4,096 multiply-adds, about 1 µs of scalar work and less in BLAS. So each call pays as much for the interpreter, arg
- *Pure Python* builds a graph of scalar `Value` objects: 59,647 nodes for a document of 7 positions, about 8,300 per position, counted in the program. Each node is an object allocation, a tuple of children and a tuple of local gradients in the forward pass, then a visit in the topological sort and a loop over children in the backward pass; Adam is a Python loop over 4,192 objects. 120 ms for 60,0
- *dzaima/APL* interprets a tree in Java. Its matrix product in these programs is a dfn, `mm←{↑(↓⍺)∘.{+/⍺×⍵}↓⍉⍵}`, which calls an interpreted function once per element of the result: about 4,000 calls in the forward pass and twice that in the backward. Its step is bound by interpreted calls per element, which is why it sits between pure Python (interpreted per scalar operation

His expectation is the usual result for larger arrays, where the BLAS kernel outruns a plain Java loop. This model is below that size. In this session NumPy's step alone went from 0.17–0.24 ms at batch 1 to 0.41 ms at batch 4, 1.41 ms at batch 16 and 2.66 ms at batch 32, about 83 µs a document at batch 32; Java's went from 0.101 ms at batch 1 to 0.404 ms at batch 4, 101 µs a document. 9	## Dispatch and overloading
10	
11	**Overloads may differ in their static parameters (P-45).** An example is `ident[\T extends Shape\](x: T): T` beside `ident[\T extends Round\](x: T): T`. The Working Draft forbids such pairs. A declaration's declared domain is the set of argument types that its declared parameter types accept at some instance within its bounds: every `Shape` for the first `ident`. The checker applies the overloading rules of `SKILL.md` to declared domains. The more specific declaration's return type must be a subtype of the other's at every instance that the argument types allow, not at one only.
12	
13	**Where a declaration has static parameters, exclusion is read over the whole tuple of parameter types (P-152).** By the exclusion rule, a value has at most one instance of a given generic type. So where both declarations name the same generic type at a position, a value of both domains makes the two static arguments equal. The domains exclude where these equalities cannot hold together, or where some position excludes at the instance that they force. So `o[\T\](x: P[\T\], b: Box[\T\])` beside `o[\T\](x: Q[\T\], b: Box[\T\])`, with `P[\T\] excludes { Q[\T\] }`, is valid. Both paths refuse a pair whose exclusion needs a static parameter that the equalities leave free, as `o[\T, U\](x: Q[\U\], b: Box[\T\])` beside the first `o`: nothing ties `U` to `T`. In its test of whether two domains exclude each other, the checker puts the meet of a static parameter's declared bounds in the parameter's place where the parameter is a whole parameter type, an element of a tuple or a member of an intersection or union (P-157). Inside a static argument, as `T` in `Box[\T\]`, the parameter stays.
14	
15	**Walk chooses by declared parameter types, never by the order of the declarations.** It compares declared domains where one lies strictly inside the other. Otherwise it compares the instances that the call makes. It infers a dotted generic method's static arguments from the arguments' run-time types, as for a generic function. A trait's generic method called with an argument outside a bound fails with "Cannot unify".
16	
17	**Walk's load check is not the verdict of these rules.** It refuses some valid pairs and loads some invalid ones, and the checker differs from it on others. Before you change code to pass walk's check, or take its acceptance as proof, find the case in `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks": a case that cites a ledger row is a departure of walk.
18	
19	**Two functional methods with equivalent parameter types are duplicates, wherever `self` stands.** So the checker refuses `f(self, y: S)` beside `f(x: S, self)` in a trait `S`. Abstract declarations count:
20	
21	- both paths refuse an abstract and a concrete method with the same parameter types in one trait;
22	- both paths refuse an object that inherits an abstract functional method from one trait and its body from another, unless the object declares the method itself (P-149). The Scala language accepts it.
23	
24	The Meet Rule asks for a declaration that covers the meet of two overloads that neither exclude each other nor nest (`SKILL.md`, "Fortress as a language"). An abstract functional method is an overload for this rule too. So the checker refuses `h(self): ZZ32` in a trait `S` beside a top-level `h(x: String): ZZ32`: nothing covers the meet of `S` and `String`. Likewise, a program's trait that declares its own functional `+` overlaps the library's `+` between an array and a number, because a type can extend both the trait and `Number`, which has no `comprises` clause (P-160). Declare the trait `excludes { Number }`, or, where the trait itself extends `Number`, `excludes { HasRank }`, the trait that arrays extend. Or declare the `+` in an object, not in a trait: an object excludes every trait that it does not extend, because no other type can extend it. Otherwise walk refuses the program at load: "fails the Meet Rule". The checker refuses such a pair in one component, but accepts it against the library's `+` (row 918). Give a trait with its own functional `-`, `MIN` or `MAX` the same fix: the library declares these in the same form.

- F-26 **Under walk, a call chooses on declared domains only where one of two applicable declarations has static parameters of its own, and otherwise compares the instances that it makes.** It builds P-45 under walk, by the rule of the `fortress-repo` skill's `revival-changes.md`, "Dispatch and overloading". A declaration has static parameters of its own if it is a generic function or constructor, or a functional method with static parameters in a trait or object without any. Where the chosen instance takes an argument only by a conversion, walk converts it and dispatches again, except at an overloaded dotted method and at a tuple converted element by element. Gated by `tests/DispatchDeclaredDomain.fss` and `DispatchConvertedAgain.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-dispatch/REPORT.md` sections 5.1 and 5.2.
- F-301 **On the compiled path, a native helper is called through a generated wrapper that unboxes and boxes, and in one measurement C2 inlined the whole call in a hot loop, so it cost nothing of its own.** A `builtinPrimitive` binding and a written `import java` call compile to the same wrapper call. Escape analysis removed every temporary box; one box stayed per assignment to a mutable variable per iteration. This held only where C2's inline depth reached each box's constructor chain: an operator called from more than 4 further inlined frames kept its temporary boxes. Observed once, on one program, while the prelude's number types were traits, not since they are value objects; no test checks it. Detail: `perf-probes/helper-calls/REPORT.md` sections 2 to 5.
- F-350 **On the compiled path, the arms of a parallel `do`, a tuple's elements, an operator's operands and a call's arguments fork through `CodeGen.genParallelExprs`, which joins every arm that it forked before an exception leaves the group.** The first exception in the arms' order leaves; an arm not yet forked does not run; a `VirtualMachineError` leaves without the joins. The one library's parallel `ZZ32` range splits only a range of more than 16 elements, so, by reading, a reduction over one of microGPT's vectors, 16, 16, 4 or 4 wide, forks nothing on either path. Tests: `compiler_tests/AlsoArmThrowsJoinsCompiled`, `tests/ParRangeGrainWalk`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-forked-arguments/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why".

content.content:
- F-21 **The February 2011 Working Draft's bare `Nothing`, `object Nothing extends Maybe[\T\] excludes Just[\T\] where {T extends Object}`, is refused on both paths.** Its `excludes` clause, which an object cannot have, is a syntax error. Without it, both paths report `T is undefined`: a `where` clause on an object binds no type variable of its `extends` clause, as for a trait (row 17, fixed). Today's specification refuses the form by instantiation exclusion, `where` clauses or not (F-167); P-90 still calls it future work that waits for such clauses. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-maybe/REPORT.md` section 5.
- F-29 **Under walk, the load check refuses a trait or object that extends a closed trait, one with a `comprises` clause, of the program's main component where the clause does not allow it.** An extender is allowed where it lies below a listed type, is a trait whose own clause lists only allowed types, or is a generic trait whose every extender lies below a listed type (`Specification/basic/traits.tex`). A check of the library's clauses would refuse every program that imports `Reflect` (row 595), and some team tests and demos (row 596). Gated by `tests/ComprisesUnlistedExtender`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-load-check/REPORT.md` section 5.
- F-291 **Under the compile command's bound `Any` (F-289), the compiled path runs generics at tuple and arrow static arguments as it did with `extends Any` written; `()` fails whatever the bound (row 339), and so does a generic operator applied to a tuple (row 1056).** Measured once over generic functions, objects, traits and their dispatch: the class loader made the same classes, so the bound costs the run time nothing there (F-292: its cost in tests). The one library's own instantiations at tuples were not run. No test gates it. Detail: `perf-probes/bound-any-compiled/REPORT.md`, "The shapes by setting".
- F-351 **A compiled transaction validates itself and every ancestor, and an abort restarts the block whose transaction it names.** A transaction records no read of its own write. `abort()` names no transaction, so the innermost block restarts; the outermost block restarts for any abort. An exit commits it (F-401). A nested commit hands its parent its reads and its writes. Open: a nested block sees a plain write by another thread that runs its outer block (row 984). Tests: `compiler_tests/AtomicNested*Compiled`, `NestedAtomicAbortCompiled`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-compiled-transaction/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why".
- F-356 **In the fork/join shape of the library and the compiled runtime, a Java model of microGPT's step on unboxed arrays runs 19 to 80 times slower than plain loops at the library's grains, and 1.4 to 4.8 times slower with the matrix product stopped at blocks of 16.** The library's grains are 16 elements for a range (P-175) and one for the matrix product. Its times, F-355's baseline on a `ForkJoinPool`, are a floor for compiled Fortress of this shape. At microGPT's sizes this shape costs time at any thread count, most of it from the matrix product's missing grain. Measured once on 4 CPUs, by `java-baseline/run.sh steps`. Detail: `java-baseline/REPORT.md` section 6.
